prompt:
A county records office keeps its birth-register index on cards, and this is the indexing bench at the end of the morning: a shallow card cabinet turned to face the room with its drawers pulled open, and the twelve surname cards that came in this morning standing in them.

The twelve surnames are fixed and they are these: SMITH, SMYTH, SMYTHE, CLARK, CLARKE, JOHNSON, JONSON, JANSEN, JANSSEN, BAKER, BACKER, BAKKER.

This office does not file by spelling. It files by the sound index, and the rule hangs on a card over the bench. Keep the first letter of the surname as it stands. Then go along the remaining letters giving each one the figure of its own group: B F P V are 1; C G J K Q S X Z are 2; D and T are 3; L is 4; M and N are 5; R is 6; and A E I O U H W Y take no figure at all. Two letters that would take the same figure and stand next to each other count once between them. The code is that first letter followed by the first three figures, made up to three figures with noughts if fewer come out.

The clerk pencils each surname's code onto its own card, under the surname, and stands every card in the drawer whose front carries that same code. One drawer is pulled open for each code that has come up this morning and none is pulled open for a code that has not. How many drawers that comes to, and which code lands on which card, is deliberately being kept from you -- that is the whole of the morning's work.

Give me the bench square to the camera with every open drawer front and every one of the twelve cards in one frame, the codes and the surnames big enough to read. The rule card is out of frame: no coding rule, no working and no tally may appear on the cards, on the drawer fronts or anywhere else on the bench.
